newsitem.title: CHINA: New GM China JV to pay capital goods duty.
newsitem.headline: New GM China JV to pay capital goods duty.

text.p: A $1.57 billion joint venture between U.S. automotive giant General Motors Corp and state-run Shanghai Automotive Industry Corp will not be exempt from a tax on imports of capital goods, company officials said on Tuesday.
White House officials earlier estimated the value of the joint venture at $1.3 billion.

Industry analysts had speculated that Beijing would grant the huge project a special waiver from a change in China's tax law that removed exemptions for foreign invested companies on imports of capital goods.
"We are very specific on the fact that there is no waiver," Rudolph Schlais, president of General Motors China Operations, told a news conference.

Company officials declined to say how much the import duty would cost the $1.57 billion Shanghai-based plant that will make medium-sized sedans, but said failure to secure a waiver would affect profits.
"Obviously, the changes in tax do affect the returns on the project," said John Smith, chairman of GM's board of directors.
"However, this is still a good programme," Smith said.
The new plant, Shanghai GM, would import nearly $1.6 billion worth of goods from the United States, Smith said but did not say what portion of that would be subject to the tax.
China abolished duty-free treatment for capital equipment importers from April 1996 but gave a 12-month grace period for projects launched before the change.
The GM project was registered after the deadline.
China has since extended that period to June 30 of this year for foreign-funded projects with investment of less than $30 million and to June 30 1998 for projects worth more than that.
